As for the deeds of the disbelievers, reduced to scattered dust according to Ali, Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan, they are all void for lack of faith. Finally, the commentators agree that the people of Paradise will have a better dwelling and resting place than the people of the Fire, while differing on the meaning of the midday rest and on the length of the reckoning.

This verse states that the disbelievers who denied the Resurrection and demanded the descent of angels or the sight of God in order to believe the Prophet ﷺ will see the angels on the day their fate is sealed. On that day there will be no glad tidings for them, and they will say, or be told, « hijran mahjuran », meaning a forbidden and utterly barred thing. The commentators differ on when this sight occurs. Ibn 'Abbas, Muqatil and 'Ata' place it at the moment of death, while Mujahid, Qatada and most others place it on the Day of Resurrection. Ibn Kathir sees no contradiction, since the angels appear to the disbelievers at both times. As for the phrase « hijran mahjuran », most exegetes, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Zamakhshari, take it to mean forbidden and prohibited: God forbids them good tidings or Paradise. Mujahid and Ibn Jurayj hold instead that the disbelievers utter it as the Arabs did when facing something hateful, seeking refuge from the angels. Al-Tabari prefers the first reading, since seeking protection is not a prohibition. The next verse declares that the deeds of the disbelievers will become scattered dust. The commentators offer several senses for « hiba' »: dust visible in a sunbeam through an opening, ashes, spilt water, or fallen leaves. The sense most favoured by the linguists is the dust seen floating in sunlight. By contrast, the people of Paradise will have a better abode and a finer resting place. Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn 'Abbas report that the reckoning will be completed around midday, and that each party will then rest in its final dwelling.

This verse says that the deeds of the disbelievers, which they thought would benefit them, will be nullified on the Day of Judgment and turned into scattered dust. The commentators agree that "qadimna" means that God purposed and turned toward their deeds, and that "hiba'" is the fine dust seen in a shaft of sunlight entering through an opening, which cannot be grasped in the hand, while "manthur" means scattered. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada and Ibn Zayd took it to mean debris of leaves and earth blown by the wind, and Ibn 'Abbas also said it is spilled water, while 'Ali, al-Hasan, 'Ikrima and Mujahid spoke of sunlight in a window, and Muqatil of dust raised by the hooves of animals. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that such deeds are void when they lack sincerity toward God or conformity to the revealed law. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi read the verb as an image of the ruin of their works rather than a literal approach. The commentators agree that the people of Paradise will have a better dwelling and a better resting place than the people of the Fire. Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas and Sa'id ibn Jubayr report that the reckoning will be finished before midday, so that the dwellers of Paradise rest in Paradise and those of the Fire rest in the Fire, while others understand the word "maqil" in the general sense of a better place of repose.

The commentators explain that the verse describes the people of Paradise on the Day of Resurrection as having a better dwelling place and a finer resting place than the polytheists who boasted of their wealth in this world. Most agree that the 'mustaqarr' is the place where they stay for most of their time, to sit and converse, and the 'maqil' is the place of midday rest. Some take the comparison as absolute, others as sarcasm toward the disbelievers, since there is no good in the abode of the Fire. Al-Tabari and Ibn 'Atiyya read it as covering the whole state of the blessed in the Hereafter compared with that of the damned. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi note that the word 'maqil' need not mean sleep, since there is no sleep in Paradise, but is a figure taken from the comfort of the wealthy who rest with their spouses. On the duration of the reckoning, Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and others report that it ends at midday, with the people of Paradise resting in Paradise and those of the Fire in the Fire, while al-Razi and al-Qurtubi mention that this may be as short as half a day of worldly time. Ibn Kathir sees in the verse a sign that the believers attained their state through accepted deeds, unlike the disbelievers who have no deed to save them.

This verse describes the Day of Judgment, when the sky is split open with clouds and the angels descend in great numbers, sovereignty that day belonging to the Most Merciful alone, and a hard day for the disbelievers. The commentators agree that the verse speaks of the Last Day and that the splitting of the sky means its opening and rupture. On the meaning of the clouds, opinions differ: Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir describe a white, thin cloud, while Mujahid and Ibn Juraij link it to the cloud in which God will come, al-Hasan sees it as a veil between heaven and earth through which the angels ascend, and al-Zamakhshari reports that it resembles a white mist that appeared only to the Children of Israel in their wandering. There is broad agreement that the angels descend to earth for the reckoning: according to Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Kathir, each heaven opens and its inhabitants descend, more numerous than those of the one below, followed by the Cherubim and the bearers of the Throne. Al-Razi considers the descent of God's Essence impossible, while Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Alusi interpret it as the descent of His command and judgment, and Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Uthaymin relate it as transmitted. On sovereignty, al-Tabari holds that all earthly kingdoms vanish save that of the Almighty. The following verse, according to most commentators, concerns 'Uqba ibn Abi Mu'it and Ubayy ibn Khalaf, but Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Uthaymin hold that it applies generally: every wrongdoer will regret following the one who led him away from the Reminder.

This part of the verse declares that on the Day of Judgment true sovereignty belongs to the All-Merciful alone, since every earthly kingdom vanishes that day, and that the day will be very hard for the disbelievers because of the torment and terror they face. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that the "true" dominion is the one that never ends, and that every other rule perishes; al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and Ibn 'Ashur read it the same way, with al-Razi adding that this sovereignty is not a matter of mere dependence or obligation.

The commentators place the verse within a description of the events of the Last Day, when the sky splits open with clouds and the angels descend. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir cite reports about the successive descent of the angels of each heaven and the coming of the Lord surrounded by the bearers of the Throne; Ibn Kathir judges many of these reports weak or doubtful, while al-Qurtubi simply transmits them. Ibn 'Ashur declines to fix the physical detail of the rift and leaves several readings open for the preposition "bi" before "al-ghamam".

On the sense of "difficult for the disbelievers", several scholars take the restriction to imply that the day is easy for believers. Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Nasafi cite a hadith saying the day will be lightened for the believer until it is lighter than a prescribed prayer; its chain is contested, yet the commentators report it without deciding. Al-Qasimi and al-Sha'rawi stress that the mercy of God is present even within the exercise of His justice.

Finally, the readings of the verb vary: Ibn Kathir and Abu Hayyan note variants of "nuzzila" and "tashaqqaqa", without changing the overall meaning of divine sovereignty and the severity of that day for the disbelievers.

This passage describes the Day of Judgement, when the wrongdoer bites his hands in regret, wishing he had taken a path with the Messenger that would have led to salvation. The commentators agree on the plain meaning: the disbeliever's remorse for having neglected faith, expressed both in speech and in gesture. They differ on who is meant. Ibn Abbas, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab and al-Sha'bi, followed by most reports cited by al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Wahidi, identify the wrongdoer as 'Uqba ibn Abi Mu'ayt and the "certain one" as his friend Ubayy ibn Khalaf or Umayya ibn Khalaf, and present this story as the occasion of revelation. Mujahid and Abu Raja' take the wrongdoer as a generic term for any wrongdoer and the "certain one" as Satan. Ibn 'Atiyya, Ibn Kathir and others hold that the wording is general and not limited to that particular case. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and al-Baydawi explain that biting the hands is a metaphor for anger and grief. On the "reminder", some take it to be the Quran, others the Prophet's admonition or the testimony of faith. Most commentaries close with a warning against a companion who leads one astray, as Al-Qurtubi and others illustrate with the hadith of the musk-carrier and the bellows-blower.

This verse describes the Day of Judgment when the wrongdoer bites his hands in regret, wishing he had followed the Messenger on the path to salvation, and then laments having taken a certain person as a close friend who led him astray from the Reminder after it had come to him. The commentators agree that biting the hands is a figure of remorse and grief, that khalil means a deep, intimate friend, and that this wish comes too late. They differ, however, on who the wrongdoer and 'so-and-so' are. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Abbas report that the wrongdoer is 'Uqba ibn Abi Mu'ayt and that 'so-and-so' is Umayya or Ubayy ibn Khalaf, following the account of the revelation in which the latter urged the former to renounce Islam. Mujahid and Abu Raja' take the wrongdoer as a general term and 'so-and-so' as Satan. Al-Razi, al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi extend the meaning to every wrongdoer and to anyone obeyed in disobedience to God. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan note that the deliberate vagueness of 'so-and-so' aims to include every misleader. The commentators agree that Satan forsakes those who follow him when hardship comes, and some attribute the final clause to the wrongdoer while others attribute it to God. The verses warn against keeping company with bad companions, as the hadith comparing the good companion to a bearer of musk illustrates. As for the Reminder, some take it to mean the Qur'an, others the testimony of faith or the Prophet's admonition.

This verse depicts a scene from the terrors of the Day of Resurrection, when the wrongdoer bites his hands in regret and anguish, wishing he had followed the Messenger and taken the path of salvation. He laments: 'Woe to me! Would that I had not taken so-and-so as a friend! He led me astray from the Reminder after it had come to me,' adding that Satan forsakes man when he is most in need. The commentators agree that biting the hands expresses remorse and grief, and the verse stresses how hard that day will be for the disbelievers. As for who the wrongdoer is, Ibn 'Abbas, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, Qatada, Mujahid, al-Sha'bi and others identify him as 'Uqba ibn Abi Mu'ayt, whose friend was Umayya or Ubayy ibn Khalaf, though Ibn 'Abbas also reports the reverse. Mujahid and Abu Raja' take the term as generic, meaning any wrongdoer, with 'so-and-so' being Satan. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn Juzayy hold that the wording is general even though the occasion of revelation was specific. Al-Razi reports the Rafidite claim that the wrongdoer's name was concealed, and rejects it. Most identify the 'Reminder' with the Qur'an, while others understand it as the Messenger's admonition or the profession of faith. Scholars also differ on whether the clause about Satan forsaking man is God's words or the wrongdoer's. The verse ultimately warns against bad companions, and commentators recall the hadith of the righteous companion and the blacksmith.

This verse records the Prophet's complaint to his Lord that his people have abandoned the Quran. Commentators differ on the meaning of "mahjur". Mujahid, al-Nakha'i and Ibn Zayd, among others, take it to mean forsaken: the people neither believed in the Quran, nor listened to it, nor acted upon it. Others, including Mujahid and al-Nakha'i in another report, understand it as foul speech and raving, claiming the Quran was magic or poetry, or making noise while it was recited so that no one could hear it. Al-Tabari prefers the first view, since God quotes their words, "Do not listen to this Quran, and make noise during its recitation", which is itself a form of abandonment. Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Qayyim list several forms of abandoning the Quran: not listening to it, not believing in it, not reflecting on it, not acting by it, not turning to it for judgment, and not seeking healing in it. Most exegetes hold that the words are a complaint made in this world, while Abu Muslim al-Isfahani considers them a statement made on the Day of Judgment. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi note that such a complaint is a warning to the people, since when prophets complained of their peoples, punishment came swiftly. The next verse consoles the Prophet: God has appointed for every prophet enemies among the criminals, and God suffices as guide and helper. According to Ibn 'Abbas, the enemy meant was Abu Jahl.

This passage records the Prophet's complaint against his people who abandoned the Qur'an, followed by the consolation that every prophet before him faced enemies among the criminals of his people, and that the Lord suffices as guide and helper. The commentators agree on the main sense of consolation and steadfastness, and that the Prophet should be patient as earlier messengers were. The meaning of "have taken this Qur'an as something abandoned" is disputed. Mujahid, al-Nakha'i, Ibn Kathir and Muqatil take it to mean that they spoke evil of it, calling it magic, poetry or raving, while Ibn Zayd, al-Tabari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Baydawi understand it as turning away from it and refusing to listen. Al-Tabari prefers the second reading, relying on the verse where the disbelievers say, do not listen to this Qur'an. Ibn Qutayba and al-Zajjaj explain hajr as useless talk. According to Ibn Abbas, the wrongdoer was 'Uqba ibn Abi Mu'ayt and his friend Ubayy ibn Khalaf, but Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn Kathir extend the verse to every wrongdoer. On the word enemy, some read it as a collective singular and others as a plural, and both are accepted. The closing promise of guidance and help is generally understood as an assurance to the Prophet and to those who follow him.

This verse records the objection of the disbelievers to the manner of the Quran's revelation: why was it not sent down all at once, as the Torah was sent to Moses? The commentators explain that its gradual revelation had a purpose, namely to strengthen the heart of the Prophet ﷺ and help him memorize and understand it. On the phrase "wa rattalnahu tartilan", Ibn Abbas and Qatada take it to mean making it clear, al-Nakha'i and al-Hasan mean revealing it piece by piece, Mujahid means one part following another, and as-Suddi means detailing it. The commentators differ on who the disbelievers were: Ibn Abbas names the Quraysh, while others point to the Jews. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir explain that the revelation came in response to events and questions, and Ibn Kathir notes that it spanned about twenty-three years. Al-Razi lists several reasons for the gradual descent: the Prophet could neither read nor write, abrogation can only apply to a text revealed in parts, gradual revelation eases the obligations, and the challenge repeated with each part strengthens the miracle. Ibn Ashur holds that revelation in parts adds to the inimitability of the text, and al-Baydawi and al-Zamakhshari add that it strengthens the proof. In the verses that follow, most commentators, including Ibn Kathir and al-Razi, take literally the image of the disbelievers dragged on their faces to Hell, while others read it as a metaphor for extreme humiliation.

This verse states that whenever the disbelievers bring the Prophet ﷺ an objection or a strange argument meant to discredit his message, God brings him the truth that refutes it, with an explanation clearer and finer than theirs. The commentators link it to the objection that the Quran was not sent down all at once. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada take tafsir here to mean explanation and detail, so God's answer is clearer than their claim. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya understand the word mathal as a strange question or a baseless pretext, which the truth overturns. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir take the truth to be the Quran itself. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi explain that gradual revelation strengthened the Prophet's heart, followed events and questions, and allowed abrogation. Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn Juzayy add that it made memorization easier. On the next verse, most commentators, including Ibn Kathir and al-Baydawi, take the image of being gathered on their faces into Hell literally, citing the hadith of Anas. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya read it as a figure of extreme humiliation. The accounts of the occasion of revelation name 'Uqba ibn Abi Mu'ayt and Ubayy ibn Khalaf, while others extend the sense to any wrongdoer who follows a companion into disobedience.

This verse states that those who disbelieved and rejected the Prophet ﷺ will be gathered on the Day of Resurrection upon their faces and driven into Hell. They occupy the worst position and are the furthest astray from the path. The commentators agree that the gathering upon the faces is to be taken literally in the view of most scholars, citing the hadith of Anas ibn Malik in which a man asks the Prophet ﷺ how this can be, and he answers that the One who made them walk on their feet in the world is able to make them walk on their faces. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Juzayy adopt this reading. Ibn Kathir links the verse to the surrounding context, where the disbelievers objected that the Quran was not sent down all at once, and explains that its gradual revelation strengthened the Prophet's heart and eased its memorising and understanding.

Others, including al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Razi, consider that walking upon the faces may be a figure of extreme humiliation and disgrace, and al-Razi and the Sufi reading see it as the hearts being attached to worldly things. Al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud mention this interpretation but find it less plausible. Most commentators hold that the verse concerns the disbelievers who asked these questions out of obstinacy, though other inhabitants of the Fire are included.

The commentators differ on the comparative phrase 'worst in position and most astray'. Many take it as a superiority over the believers, while al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud take the Prophet ﷺ as the standard of comparison, in the manner of 'Shall I tell you who is worse in recompense with Allah?'. Ibn 'Ashur reads the comparative as an intensifier rather than a true comparison.

This verse recounts the story of Moses: God gave him the Book (the Torah) and appointed his brother Aaron as a wazir, meaning helper and supporter. God commanded them to go to Pharaoh and his people, who had denied Our signs; they denied the two messengers, and God utterly destroyed them. The commentators agree that the passage consoles the Prophet ﷺ and warns the Quraysh polytheists that the same fate may befall them as befell the nations that rejected their messengers. At-Tabari, al-Baghawi, Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Atiyya hold that the text contains an ellipsis, meaning: they went, they were denied, and We destroyed them. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Zamakhshari say the story is abridged, keeping only its two ends, which are its essence. Al-Razi, al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud note that being a wazir does not contradict prophethood, since several prophets could be sent in the same time and support one another. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Kathir state that the destruction was by drowning. Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn Kathir explain that the people of Noah, by rejecting Noah, rejected all messengers. Opinions differ on the People of the Rass: Ibn 'Abbas says they were the people of a well in Azerbaijan, Qatada that they were from a town in Yamama, Ka'b, Muqatil and al-Suddi that they were at a well in Antioch where Habib the carpenter was killed; al-Tabari favours that they were the People of the Trench, while Ibn Kathir finds the narrations about them weak. All agree that the people of Sodom were destroyed by stones, and that the Quraysh passed by their ruins without taking heed, because they did not hope for resurrection. The verse thus teaches that belief in resurrection leads to reflection.

The plain meaning of the verse, as the commentators explain it, is that God recounts the story of Moses and his brother Aaron. He gave Moses the Book (the Torah) and appointed Aaron as a helper and supporter, then commanded them to go to Pharaoh and his people, who had denied God's signs. They went, were rejected, and God utterly destroyed them. All the commentators agree that the sentence contains an implied part: they went, the people denied them, and We destroyed them. The story is abridged, mentioning only its beginning and end, because the purpose is to establish the proof through the sending of messengers and the right to destruction through denial. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir identify the people as the Copts, and al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and al-Baydawi explain that being a vizier does not contradict prophethood, since several prophets could be sent at the same time and support one another. Regarding the past tense of the verb "denied", al-Razi and Ibn Ashur read it as a reference to the Quraysh of Mecca, as a warning and a preparation for the threatened destruction. Recitation variants are also mentioned: Ali and al-Hasan read "fa-dammiraa-hum" as an imperative, and another reading adds emphasis, while Abu Hayyan and Ibn Atiyya discuss their status. Scholars agree that the verse consoles the Prophet and warns his people that the fate of the nations who denied could befall them.

The commentators place this verse within the account of the fates of the nations who denied their messengers. Its plain meaning is that the people of Noah were drowned because they rejected Noah, and that this drowning was made a sign for mankind, while a painful punishment is prepared for the wrongdoers. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Atiyya, al-Razi, al-Qurtubi and Abu Hayyan agree on this general sense. They differ on the grammar of the phrase 'and the people of Noah': some take it as an object of a hidden verb repeated by 'We drowned them', others as coordinated with the pronoun in 'We destroyed them'. The meaning is unaffected. On the phrase 'the messengers', al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Atiyya and al-Razi explain that denying one prophet amounts to denying all of them, since they share the same core message. Al-Tabari notes that 'the wrongdoers' means the unbelievers. In the following verse, the commentators discuss the People of the Rass: Ibn Abbas and Qatada speak of a people of Thamud or a village in Yamama, al-Tabari favours the People of the Trench, and Ibn Kathir relays these views while noting the weakness of some reports. Al-Tabari defines rass as any dug well and its people as those who buried their prophet in it. Several scholars note that God destroys no people before sending messengers and warnings. Modern commentaries, such as those of al-Sha'rawi and Ibn 'Uthaymin, read the passage as consolation for the Prophet and a warning to the Quraysh.

This verse recalls peoples whom God destroyed for rejecting their messengers: 'Ad, Thamud, the People of the Rass, and many generations between them, whose number only God knows. The commentators explain that the apparent meaning is the announcement of their destruction, meant as a warning to the Quraysh against a similar fate. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi note that in Arabic rass means an unlined well, or any excavation such as a well, mine or grave, and that the exact identity of the People of the Rass is uncertain. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada and 'Ikrima relate them to a people from Thamud or the inhabitants of a place in al-Yamama, while Ka'b, Muqatil and al-Suddi identify them with the people of Antioch who killed Habib al-Najjar. Al-Tabari favours the view that they are the People of the Trench mentioned in Surat al-Buruj. Ibn Kathir considers it wiser to keep to the general statement since God did not specify them. On the word qarn, opinions differ on its length: forty, seventy or one hundred and twenty years, though most take it to mean a contemporary generation. The commentators stress that God destroys no community before establishing proof against it through examples and warnings. Ibn 'Ashur explains that tabbara means to break into pieces and utterly ruin. All see these accounts as a consolation to the Prophet and a warning to his people.

This verse from Surah al-Furqan speaks of what God did to earlier peoples who rejected their messengers. God set forth examples for each nation, meaning instructive stories and warnings, and removed every excuse before destroying them after they persisted in denial. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Ashur agree that tabbir means to break or crush, that is, to annihilate completely, and that the examples are the proofs and lessons. The preceding verses recalled the fate of several peoples: Pharaoh's people, Noah's people who were drowned, ‘Ad and Thamud, the People of the Rass, and many generations in between. On the People of the Rass the commentators differ widely. Ibn ‘Abbas and Ibn Jurayj say they were a people of Thamud; Qatada says they were the people of a town in al-Yamama called al-Falaj; al-Tabari describes them as a people who sat around a well; Ibn Jarir prefers that they were the People of the Trench mentioned in Surah al-Buruj; Ka‘b, Muqatil and al-Suddi identify them with the people of Antioch who killed Habib the carpenter. Ibn Kathir and al-Tabari consider the narrations used to identify them weak and do not accept them as proof. On the word qarn, the scholars range between forty, seventy, one hundred and one hundred and twenty years, and often take it to mean a community living in the same era. The question “Had they not seen it?” refers to the Quraysh who passed by the town of Lot on their trade journeys to Syria; al-Baghawi, al-Razi and Ibn Kathir explain that they did not take heed because they did not hope for resurrection. Grammatical discussion also concerns the accusative of kullan and the tanwin of ‘Adan and Thamud.

God tells us that the Quraysh, on their trading journeys to Syria, passed by the town that was rained upon with a terrible rain of stones, namely Sodom, one of the towns of the people of Lot, yet they saw it with their own eyes and took no lesson from it. The commentators report that there were five such towns, of which only one was spared because its people did not commit the vile deed, and that Abraham had warned them. They agree that the 'rain of evil' refers to the stones that fell upon them, and that the question in the verse is a rebuke. As for their failure to reflect, most explain it by their lack of hope in the resurrection: they did not fear the reckoning nor hope for reward. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya understand 'hope' here as expectation or desire, while al-Tabari and others take it to mean 'fear', following the Tihamah dialect. The commentators connect the verse to the preceding accounts of peoples who rejected their messengers and were destroyed after warning, and to the mockery of the pagans toward the Prophet ﷺ. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi report that the Quraysh would scornfully say: 'Is this the one God has sent as a messenger?' Several commentators note that the polytheists clung to the worship of their idols, and Ibn Abbas and others see the one who follows his desire as taking his desire as a god. The verse brings consolation to the Prophet ﷺ and a warning to those who reject him, that they should not suffer the fate of earlier peoples.

This verse describes how the disbelievers, when they see the Prophet ﷺ, treat him only as an object of mockery, saying with contempt: "Is this the one whom God has sent as a messenger?" They add that he almost led them away from their gods had they not been steadfast in worshipping them. The commentators agree on the plain sense of mockery and belittling, and that these words come from stubbornness rather than from argument. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir report that the speaker was Abu Jahl or a group of idolaters, and several understand the word "sabr" as perseverance in idol worship. On the phrase "he almost led us astray", al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi see evidence of the Prophet's ﷺ intense effort to call them, to the point of almost winning them over, while al-Razi notes that the remark in fact shows they recognised the force of his argument. All agree on the warning in "they will know, when they see the punishment, who is further astray", meaning that they will realise their error only at the moment of punishment. The passage then turns to the one who takes his own desire as his god: Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid relate that this refers to a man who worshipped a stone and abandoned it whenever he found a finer one, while al-Tabari extends the meaning to anyone who follows his desires. Al-Kalbi holds that this verse was abrogated by the verse on fighting, whereas others regard it as still in force. Finally, the text states that most of them neither listen to understand nor reason, that they are like cattle, and even more misguided, since cattle follow the one who tends them and know their pasture, whereas they submit neither to their Lord nor to what benefits them.

Verse 25:42 reports the mocking words of the idolaters about the Prophet ﷺ: he nearly led us away from our gods, they say, had we not stood firm in worshipping them; but they will know, when they see the punishment, who is further astray in the way. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi explain that 'had we not persevered' means that the idolaters held firmly to the worship of their idols, and they read the closing part as a divine threat. Al-Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan and al-Baydawi see in the same words a proof of how hard the Prophet strove to call his people, and how close they came, in their own estimation, to abandoning their religion, were it not for their stubbornness. Al-Zamakhshari holds that these words were spoken in mockery, and that God's reply cuts short their argument by pointing to the punishment. Ibn 'Atiyya adds that the verse also consoles the Prophet. Al-Razi notes that the idolaters never offered a reasoned objection to the proofs, relying only on denial and the blind imitation of their forefathers. As to who is 'further astray', al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir take it as straying from the path, while Ibn al-Jawzi takes it as going wrong about the way of guidance. The commentators generally link the punishment to the battle of Badr, to the punishment of the Hereafter, or to both.

Verse 43 of Surah al-Furqan describes the man who takes his own desire as his god, following his whims in everything he does and turning away from proof and argument. God asks His Prophet, "Have you seen him?", and then asks whether he could be his guardian, "Would you be responsible for him?". Ibn Abbas explains that a polytheist would worship a stone and, when he found a finer one, cast away the first and worship the second. Al-Hasan and Qatada broaden the meaning to anyone who follows every desire he has, whether he worships idols or commits sins. Some commentators hold that the desire itself is taken as a deity worshipped besides God, while others understand that obeying one's desire as if it were a god amounts to the same thing.

The next verse compares such people to cattle, indeed even more misguided, since cattle follow their herder and avoid what harms them, whereas these people do not submit to their Lord or acknowledge His blessings. The commentators agree that the verses console the Prophet over his people's rejection, since guidance belongs to God alone and the Prophet's duty is only to deliver the message. Al-Kalbi said the verse was abrogated by the verse of fighting, while al-Qurtubi held that it was not abrogated, since it serves as consolation to the Prophet.

These verses belong to a passage in which the polytheists mocked the Prophet, saying "Is this the one God has sent as a messenger?", and claimed he nearly led them away from their gods. God warns that they will know, when they see the punishment, who was the most astray.

This verse rebukes those who turn away from the truth although they are capable of understanding it. Al-Tabari explains that it is a question addressed to the Prophet: do you think that most of the idolaters listen to what is recited to them with real attention, or reflect on the proofs of God they witness? He compares them to cattle that do not grasp what is said to them, yet he judges them more astray than cattle, since a beast finds its pasture and obeys its keeper, whereas they do not obey their Creator nor thank Him for His favours. The commentators agree that the verse condemns the people of Makkah and consoles the Prophet. Al-Mawardi and Ibn al-Jawzi note that the word 'most' allows for some who recognised the truth but were held back by love of leadership, as al-Razi and al-Nasafi also say. Ibn al-Jawzi, Ibn Juzayy and Ibn Kathir explain why they are worse than cattle: cattle recognise who does them good and who harms them, seek what benefits them and avoid what harms them, whereas these people neglect the greatest benefit, which is reward, and do not fear the greatest harm, which is punishment. Al-Razi adds that the ignorance of cattle harms no one, whereas the ignorance of these people corrupts others. Al-Qurtubi understands 'hearing' as listening in order to accept, and 'understanding' as reflecting on what is said. Some add that cattle are not held accountable, whereas these people are, which makes their error graver.

This verse points to a sign of God's power in shade: He extends it and spreads it out from dawn until sunrise, and had He willed, He would have made it fixed and unmoving. Then He made the sun a guide to the shade, since things are known by their opposites, and through the sun the shade gradually shrinks until it disappears. The commentators agree that the verse shows God's greatness, wisdom and mercy toward His servants, and that He alone deserves worship. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and others report from Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada that the shade here means the period between dawn and sunrise, that 'stillness' means permanence and not vanishing, and that the 'easy withdrawal' is swift, hidden or gradual. Al-Mawardi and al-Qurtubi hold that this withdrawal may occur at sunrise or at sunset, while Ibn Jarir takes the shade to be the shade of the night after sunset. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi explain that the shade stretches so that people may benefit from it, that the sun follows the shade as a guide leads a traveller, and that the mention of withdrawal may point to the shade's disappearance at the Hour. Ibn Ashur sees in the image a parallel with the gradual revelation of the Qur'an. Ibn al-Qayyim notes that these changes help determine the times of prayer and cool what the sun has scorched. Overall, the commentators agree on the blessing of shade and its alternation with sunlight, but differ on its precise duration and on the meaning of the withdrawal.

The commentators explain that this verse draws attention to the phenomenon of shade. According to most of them, the extended shade (al-zill al-mamdud) is the period between dawn and sunrise, a shade without the sun's rays, as reported by Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada. Others take it to mean the whole night, or the shadow of every object when the sun rises, which shrinks gradually. "Had He willed, He would have made it still" means the shade would have stayed fixed and never disappeared, according to Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada and Ibn Zayd. "Then We made the sun its guide" means the sun reveals the shade and makes it known, since things are recognised by their opposites, as al-Tabari, al-Razi and Ibn Kathir say. As for "then We draw it in to Us, a gradual drawing-in", Ibn Abbas understands it as swift, Mujahid and Qatada as imperceptible, and others as a gradual contraction. Al-Zamakhshari and those who follow him see it rather as the removal of the luminaries on the Day of Resurrection. All agree that this gradual process brings many benefits to people. Al-Razi sees in it a proof of God's power and wisdom, while Ibn Ashur sees an image of the gradual revelation of the Qur'an. Most conclude that the verse invites reflection on the blessing of shade and on the power of the Creator.

This verse says that God made the night a covering that wraps people in its darkness as a garment does, made sleep a rest that cuts off the body's exertion, and made the day a time when people spread out across the earth to seek their livelihood. The commentators differ on the meaning of 'subat'. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi, like most scholars, take it to mean rest and the halting of movement, while al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and al-Nasafi understand it as death, arguing from its contrast with 'nushur' (resurrection). Al-Baydawi and Ibn 'Atiyya allow both readings. As for 'nushur', al-Tabari, Mujahid, Qatada and Ibn Kathir, followed by Ibn al-Jawzi, read it as dispersing to earn one's living, whereas al-Tabari and Ibn 'Atiyya also allow the meaning of resurrection, which al-Razi and al-Zamakhshari adopt as a picture of sleep and waking. Many quote Luqman's saying to his son: as you sleep and are woken, so you die and are raised. Al-Qurtubi notes that night serves as a garment for concealment, though this does not excuse covering the body in prayer. Ibn 'Ashur finds the sense of rest better suited to the context of divine favour.

This verse states that God alone sends the winds as heralds before His mercy, which is the rain, and sends down from the sky a pure water. The commentators explain that the winds stir and fertilise the clouds, after which the rain falls. The word tahur means, for al-Shafi'i and most scholars, a water that purifies others, while Abu Hanifa takes it to mean pure in itself. Through this water God revives a dead, parched land and gives drink to livestock and people.

The commentators agree that rain is a divine blessing that calls for gratitude. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi report, on the authority of Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn Abbas, that the total amount of rain does not vary from year to year, but God distributes it among regions as He wills. Ibn Kathir also cites the hadith of Zayd ibn Khalid about the one who says "we were watered by such-and-such a star", who is thereby a disbeliever in God. Ikrima sees this kind of speech in the ingratitude of most people mentioned at the end of the verse.

Opinions differ on several points. Al-Razi and Ibn Kathir emphasise that tahur signifies what purifies, relying on the verse in al-Anfal. Al-Qurtubi discusses at length the rules for water that has been soiled and for used water, setting out the positions of Malik, Abu Hanifa and al-Shafi'i without deciding between them. As for the word anasi, Sibawayh regards it as the plural of insan, whereas al-Farra', al-Mubarrad and al-Zajjaj regard it as the plural of insi. Al-Alusi notes that the readings al-riyah in the plural and al-rih in the singular are both mutawatir, and he does not give preference to either.

The commentators explain that the verse recalls God's favour in sending winds that herald rain and in sending down pure, purifying water from the sky, to bring a dead, parched land back to life with vegetation and to give drink to many cattle and people. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn Atiyya and al-Baydawi largely agree that the water from heaven is rain, and they explain the order of the blessings: the revival of the land comes before watering the livestock and then the people, because human life depends on the life of the land and the herds. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Ashur note that livestock are mentioned because they are a person's wealth and their benefits are tied to him, while the word "many" points to variety and abundance; people living beside rivers are generally independent of rain, so the reference to numbers mainly concerns the inhabitants of the desert. On recitation, most read "nusqiyahu" with a damma, while Umar and Asim read it with a fatha; the plural "anasi" is analysed as the plural of insi according to al-Farra', al-Mubarrad and al-Zajjaj, or of insan according to Sibawayh. Al-Razi and al-Jassas draw from the word "tahur" a principle of purification by water and discuss at length, without settling them, the differences among Abu Hanifa, al-Shafi'i and Malik on the meaning of "tahur" and on the rules for water whose qualities have changed. As for "We distributed it among them", most exegetes, including Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Ibn Kathir, take the pronoun to refer to the rain, which God distributes each year in fixed measure among regions; they report that the ingratitude mentioned is saying that rain fell because of a certain star, as Ikrima said and as a hadith in Muslim relates. Al-Tabari and Ibn Atiyya also mention that the pronoun may refer to the Quran, al-Zamakhshari to the discourse just mentioned, and other views are reported by al-Baydawi and al-Alusi.

The commentators explain that this verse concerns the rain that God sends down from the sky. He distributes it among people, sending it to one land and not another, and in varied forms such as heavy downpour, light drizzle and fine mist, so that people would remember God's favour and be grateful. Yet most people refuse and persist in ingratitude. Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud, 'Ikrima, Mujahid, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi take the pronoun to refer to the water sent down from heaven, and the distribution to mean that God shares out rain among regions and years as He wills: no year is rainier than another overall, but the rain is spread among different lands. Several link this to an authentic hadith that whoever says 'we were watered by such-and-such a star' has disbelieved, and 'Ikrima takes this to be the ingratitude meant. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi, al-Nasafi and Abu al-Su'ud understand the verse as referring to the whole sign, the formation of clouds and the descent of rain, set out in the Qur'an and other scriptures, so that people reflect and recognise the favour, with rebellion meaning denying or neglecting it. Ibn Juzayy, al-Alusi and others allow that the pronoun may refer to the Qur'an, given the context. Al-Razi prefers a return to the rain as the nearer antecedent, and, like al-Alusi, distinguishes between one who attributes rain to the stars as independent causes, who is a disbeliever, and one who sees them as signs God created, who is not, while opinions differ on whether this is a sin. Some also read in it a consolation for the Prophet, urging him to persevere and strive with the Qur'an, since God chose him rather than sending a warner to every town.

This verse says that God could have sent a warner to every town, but chose instead to entrust the warning of all the towns to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, honouring him above the other messengers and asking him for steadfastness and effort. The commentators largely agree on this plain meaning. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Baghawi and al-Nasafi explain that the burden was lightened for him by sending one messenger, and was instead placed on him, so that through his patience he would earn a high rank with God. Regarding the command not to obey the disbelievers, most take it as a refusal to follow or accommodate them in what they demand, above all the worship of their idols, while al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan see it as a stirring of the Prophet and the believers. On the words «struggle against them with it, a great struggle», al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baydawi and al-Qurtubi hold that the pronoun refers to the Quran, Ibn Zayd to Islam, and al-Mawardi also mentions the sword, which al-Qurtubi considers unlikely since the sourah is Meccan. Al-Razi and al-Nasafi explain the greatness of this struggle by its gathering all the efforts owed to every town, and al-Baydawi by the difficulty of reasoning with stubborn opponents. The shared sense is a sustained effort at persuasion through argument.

The commentators explain that the verse addresses the Prophet ﷺ: had God willed, He could have sent a warner to every town to lighten his burden, but He entrusted him alone with warning all the cities, honouring him above the other messengers. He is therefore told not to obey the disbelievers in what they ask of him, such as compromising on the faith, and to strive against them with the Qur'an with a great striving. On the pronoun 'with it', most, including Ibn 'Abbas, al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir, refer it to the Qur'an, while Ibn Zayd takes it to mean Islam. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Atiyya find the sense of fighting with the sword remote, since the surah is Meccan. Abu Hayyan and al-Qasimi understand the striving as persistent preaching, argument and refusing to yield to them. Al-Razi and al-Baydawi explain the greatness of this striving by the difficulty of confronting the foolish with proofs, harder than the sword, and by the Prophet being sent to all cities. Ibn al-Qayyim ranks striving with the Qur'an among the highest forms of jihad. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Tabari see the command as an exhortation to the Prophet and the believers, while Ibn 'Ashur holds that the prohibition rules out even the slightest concession. Some commentaries add narratives that do not bear directly on the meaning of the verse.

The commentators explain that this verse describes a blessing of God in the two seas: one fresh and sweet, the other intensely salty, set side by side so that they do not mix and one does not spoil the other. Most agree that the word marraja means to let loose and to mix. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi understand it as letting them run in their courses or placing them side by side, while Mujahid and al-Dahhak say one pours over the other, and Ibn 'Atiyya holds that the sweet water runs through the land and the salt water surrounds it. On the identity of the two seas, Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Jubayr say they are the sea of the sky and the sea of the earth, al-Hasan says the sea of Persia and the sea of Rome, but most take them to mean sweet water and salt water in general. As for the barzakh, most describe an unseen barrier made by God's power; al-Hasan and Ibn Zayd take it to be the dry land between them, and al-Tabari holds that the barrier and the forbidden partition prevent their mixing. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and Abu Hayyan read "hijran mahjuran" as a metaphor, as if each sea seeks refuge from the other. On the following verse about the creation of man from water, Ali distinguishes nasab, what one may not marry, from sihr, what one may marry; al-Dahhak counts seven kinds of nasab and five of sihr, and some include fostering within sihr. The commentators conclude by recalling God's power and oneness.

This verse reminds us that God created the human being from water, that is, from a drop of semen, and then divided people into two kinds: males, to whom one is linked by descent, and females, through whom one is linked by marriage. It ends by affirming that your Lord is capable of all things. Most commentators understand the water as semen, while al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Ashur also see it as the origin of every living thing. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and Ibn Kathir explain that the division into nasab and sihr refers to males and females. On the meaning of the two terms opinions differ. 'Ali said that nasab is what may not be married and sihr what may be married, while Ibn Kathir treats nasab as blood kinship and sihr as an alliance resembling it. Ibn 'Atiyya and the scholars cited by al-Qurtubi count nursing relationships under nasab, whereas al-Dahhak and Tawus place them under sihr. Al-Mawardi and Ibn al-Jawzi note that sihr originally means mixing, since marriages blend families. Ibn Sirin said the verse was revealed concerning the Prophet and 'Ali, whose bond was both kinship and marriage, but this view is not universal. Al-Shinqiti reports the scholarly debate on a daughter born of adultery without settling the general question.

This verse describes how the disbelievers worship, besides God, things that can neither benefit them if they worship them nor harm them if they abandon them, and that the disbeliever thereby becomes a helper (zahir) of Satan against his Lord. Al-Tabari, Mujahid, Ibn Kathir, al-Hasan and al-Zajjaj understand the word as meaning a helper or supporter, with the disbeliever aiding Satan in disobedience to God through polytheism and hostility. Ibn Abbas, cited by al-Tabari and al-Wahidi, reports that the verse refers to Abu Jahl, while al-Qurtubi, al-Razi and al-Baydawi consider that the term "disbeliever" covers all disbelievers, since the general wording outweighs the particular occasion of revelation. Another reading, defended by al-Tabari, Abu Ubayda, al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Ashur, derives the word from the idea of casting something behind one's back, so that the disbeliever would be despised before God. Al-Tabari judges this reading less sound, since the context condemns their act rather than describing their lowliness. Ibn al-Qayyim links the notion of support to a kind of alliance with God's enemy, and Ibn Ashur notes that this act shows ingratitude towards the Master. Most commentators connect the verse with the signs of divine power mentioned just before it.

The commentators explain that God sent the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ as a bearer of good news to those who believe and obey, promising them reward and Paradise, and as a warner to those who deny and disobey, threatening them with punishment and the Fire. Most exegetes, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Razi and al-Qurtubi, take the verse to limit his mission to these two roles, and they note that he was not charged with forcing people to believe. The next verse states that he asks no wage for delivering the message. Al-Tabari and Ibn al-Jawzi understand the exception as spending wealth in God's cause, while Ibn Kathir reads it as the path of righteousness and obedience. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi explain the exception as meaning that the benefit of faith returns to the believers themselves. Al-Tabari and Ibn 'Atiyya regard the exception as disconnected from what precedes, meaning: but whoever wishes to take a path to his Lord may do so. The passage then commands the Prophet to rely on the Living who never dies and to glorify Him. Ibn Kathir explains glorification as worship and gratitude, while al-Baghawi gives the phrase 'Glory be to God and praise be to God'. Opinions differ on the referent of 'bihi' in 'ask about Him as one who knows': Ibn 'Abbas said Gabriel, Mujahid said God, and others said the Qur'an. On the word 'zahir' in the previous verse, Mujahid and Ibn Zayd read it as a helper of Satan, whereas al-Tabari reads it as meaning contemptible. All agree that the passage consoles the Prophet, whose task is to convey the message rather than to guide people.

In this verse God tells the Prophet ﷺ to say that he asks no payment from his people for conveying the message. Al-Tabari and those who follow him explain the phrase "except for whoever wills to take a way to his Lord" as meaning: whoever among you wishes to draw near to his Lord by spending in His cause and in obedience to Him may do so. Most exegetes, including Ibn Kathir, read this as a disconnected exception, since the point is not that people give anything to the Prophet but that they take the path of guidance through their own spending. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi, al-Baydawi, Abu al-Su'ud and al-Alusi take the exception as connected in a figurative sense: God has presented the fruit of faith and obedience in the form of a reward, as if the Prophet regarded the guidance of his people as his wage, in order to remove any suspicion of greed and to show extreme compassion. Ibn Juzayy and al-Qurtubi offer another reading, supplying an omitted word so that it means "except the reward of whoever…". Ibn Kathir understands the way as the path and method brought by the Prophet. Several commentators also discuss the particle "min" in "min ajr" and its grammatical status, and the occasions of revelation of neighbouring verses, but for them the core concern is the call to faith and the absence of any demand for money. Nearly all agree that relying upon the Living One who never dies, and glorifying Him, are the support that enables the Prophet to bear his people's denial.

In this verse God commands His Prophet ﷺ to rely upon the Living who never dies, that is, to entrust his affair to Him and trust Him to ward off the evil of the polytheists and to be independent of their reward. He is also told to glorify God, declaring Him free from every deficiency while praising Him for His perfect attributes. The verse concludes that God suffices as the One who knows the sins of His servants: nothing is hidden from Him, and He will requite them for these sins. The commentators agree that true everlasting life belongs to God alone, so trusting Him alone is right, since every other living being dies and whoever relies on it is left without support. Al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi explain that tasbih may mean prayer or the phrase 'Glory be to God and praise be to Him'. Ibn Kathir and al-Tha'alibi take it as an acknowledgement of God's blessings, and Ibn 'Atiyya cites the hadith promising forgiveness to whoever says it a hundred times. Al-Sam'ani and al-Zamakhshari read the closing words as a threat, whereas al-Nasafi and al-Baydawi also see a consolation for the Prophet facing unbelief. Scholars differ on the meaning of 'khabir': some take it to refer to God Himself, while others give different interpretations. Ibn al-Qayyim adds that true reliance on God does not mean abandoning the means, but taking them while trusting in Him.

This verse states that God created the heavens, the earth and all that lies between them in six days, then established Himself upon the Throne, the Most Merciful, and it tells the listener to ask about Him one who is well informed. Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Nasafi agree that these days are days of this world in their measure, since there was no sun yet, and that istiwa' means rising above the Throne, its manner being unknown. Ibn Kathir and al-Zamakhshari report that the first day was Sunday and the last Friday. Al-Qurtubi relates from Sa'id ibn Jubayr that God created in stages although He could have created in an instant, to teach His servants gentleness and deliberation. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi hold that the number six rests on a wisdom we do not know.

The commentators differ on the preposition in «fas'al bihi khabiran». Al-Zajjaj and al-Akhfash take it to mean «about», so the sense is: ask about Him someone who knows Him. Al-Kalbi takes the khabir to be God Himself, Ibn 'Abbas says it is Gabriel, and others say it is the learned among the People of the Book. Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that if you ask Him, you will find Him informed of everything, and al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya see this as an emphatic construction.

Al-Wahidi, al-Baghawi and Ibn 'Atiyya relate that the Quraysh did not know the name al-Rahman and took it to be the name of Musaylima, who was called Rahman al-Yamama. Tabari notes that the readings «ta'muruna» and «ya'muruna» are both transmitted and both valid.

The commentators explain that the verse describes the response of the disbelievers when they are called to prostrate to the Most Merciful: they feign ignorance of this name, asking "And what is the Most Merciful?", and then refuse to prostrate to what the Prophet commands them, which only increases their aversion. Most exegetes report that the Quraysh did not know "al-Rahman" as a divine name, or pretended not to, and that Musaylima the liar was called "the Rahman of Yamama", so they supposed the name referred to him; al-Baghawi, Ibn Kathir and Abu Hayyan transmit this view. Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn 'Ashur see instead a deliberate evasion and obstinacy, since the word is Arabic and its sense of intense mercy was known; Ibn 'Ashur holds that the prostration meant is the acknowledgment of divine unity, not the ritual prayer. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn al-'Arabi believe they ignored the attribute rather than the one described, while al-Razi lists three possibilities: ignorance, denial, or recognition of the name combined with refusal. The readings differ on "yamurunā": Hamza and al-Kisa'i read it in the third person, referring to Muhammad or to the Most Merciful, while the others read the second person, addressing the Prophet. All agree that this verse is a place of prostration for the reciter and listener.

Blessed is He who placed constellations in the sky, and placed in it a lamp and a luminous moon. The commentators explain that the word burûj may mean great stars, according to Mujahid, Qatada, al-Hasan and Abu Salih, or guarded palaces in the sky, according to Atiyya al-Awfi, Ibrahim al-Nakha'i and al-A'mash. Ibn 'Abbas, as reported by Ibn Kathir and al-Zamakhshari, takes them to be the twelve zodiac signs, the stations of the wandering planets, and Ibn Kathir notes that both meanings may be combined. The reading sirajan in the singular refers to the sun for most reciters, while Hamza and al-Kisa'i read surujan in the plural, which al-Tabari and al-Baghawi treat as an accepted reading with its own sense. Most scholars say the moon is mentioned separately out of honour. The word khilfa is explained by Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan and Qatada as the succession of night and day, so that what is missed in one may be made up in the other, by Mujahid as their difference in colour, and by Ibn Zayd as each one following the other. The commentators link this alternation to remembrance and gratitude, and they cite 'Umar, who made up in the day the prayers he had missed at night.

The commentators explain that God made night and day succeed one another, each taking the place of the other, and that this alternation is both a favour and a sign of His power. Umar ibn al-Khattab, al-Hasan, Ibn Abbas and Qatada, as reported by al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi, understood that what a person misses in one of the two periods can be made up in the other, which benefits whoever wishes to remember or to give thanks. Mujahid instead took the word khilfa to mean difference of colour, one white and the other black. Al-Tabari and others hold that it means succession, and cite Zuhayr's line describing herds that follow one another. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Atiyya and al-Baghawi note that the phrase 'for whoever wishes' means the verse benefits the one who reflects on their alternation and so recognises God's great power, and that gratitude consists of resting at night and acting by day. Al-Tabari and al-Razi mention two readings of the verb 'to remember', one with doubling and one without, and consider them close in meaning. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi report that the gratitude may refer to voluntary acts beyond the obligatory ones, and some say the verse was revealed concerning Umar. The commentators agree that night and day are a sign calling for remembrance and gratitude, but they differ on the precise meaning of khilfa.

This verse describes the servants of the Most Merciful, who walk on the earth with calm, dignity and humility. The commentators differ on the meaning of hawnan. Mujahid and Ikrima take it as serenity and gravity, Ibn Abbas as obedience, chastity and humility, al-Hasan as forbearance and knowledge, and Ibn Zayd as not being arrogant, oppressive or corrupt. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi note that the walking may be literal or a figure for how they deal with people. As for the phrase 'and when the ignorant address them, they say: peace', the commentators agree that it means not answering foolishness with foolishness, but speaking words that keep them free from sin and offence, which some call the 'peace of parting'. Mujahid understands it as sound, upright speech, while al-Hasan takes it as the ordinary greeting. Ibn Kathir and others reject the claim that the verse was abrogated by the verse of fighting, since patience with the foolish is praiseworthy in every case. Ibn Kathir reports that al-Hasan said this describes their days, and the next verse, 'those who spend the night prostrate and standing before their Lord', describes their nights. Ibn Abbas adds that whoever prays two or more units at night has spent the night prostrate and standing. The following verses mention their prayer to be spared the punishment of hell, their moderation in spending, their avoidance of polytheism, killing and adultery, and the promise that God changes the evil deeds of the one who repents and does good.

This verse describes the servants of the Most Merciful who spend the night before their Lord, alternating prostrations and standing. Commentators explain that the word 'spending the night' means being overtaken by night, whether one sleeps or not, so the meaning is that they devote all or most of the night to prayer. The prostration is made on the face and the standing on the feet. Ibn 'Abbas, followed by many others, held that whoever prays two or more units after the 'isha' prayer falls within this description, while al-Kalbi specified two units after maghrib and four after 'isha'. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi considered it more apparent that the verse praises them for spending most of the night in worship. Several scholars explain that prostration is mentioned before standing for the sake of the verse's rhythm and because prostration is the state in which the servant is closest to his Lord. Al-Hasan al-Basri saw this verse as describing their nights, after the previous verses describing their days. Ibn 'Ashur explained that the two terms refer to the two pillars of prayer, so the meaning is that they pray at night. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir stress that the verse encourages night prayer and the fear of God.

This verse describes the servants of the Most Merciful who spend their nights prostrating and standing in prayer, then ask God to turn away from them the torment of Hell, because its torment is constant and clings to those who suffer it. The commentators read this supplication as a sign of deep fear and humility despite their devotion, since they do not rely on their deeds alone. Most agree that the word gharaman means a relentless, lasting torment that never leaves its victim, like a creditor who will not let go of his debtor. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi report the saying of al-Hasan al-Basri that every creditor eventually parts from his debtor except the creditor of Hell. Ibn Abbas, as cited by al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, explained it as painful and grievous, while al-Zajjaj and al-Tha'alibi took it to mean the worst of torments, Abu 'Ubayda took it as destruction, and Ibn Zayd as evil. Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi relates that God demanded from the disbelievers the price of His blessings, and since they did not pay, He made them debtors and cast them into the Fire.

On the phrase that Hell is evil as a place of settling and of dwelling, most commentators, including al-Tabari, al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Kathir, hold that the two words mean much the same and reinforce each other. Al-Razi and Abu Hayyan, however, distinguish them: the settling would be for sinful believers who stay there briefly, and the dwelling for the disbelievers who remain forever. Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan allow that these words may be God's own speech, while others take them as the supplicants' own words quoted back.

The commentators explain that this verse belongs to the description of the servants of the Most Merciful, who spend their nights in prayer, alternating prostration and standing, and then beseech their Lord in fear to turn away from them the punishment of Hell, because its torment is constant and never leaves those who suffer it. The phrase "it is an evil dwelling and an evil abode" means that Hell is a wretched place to settle in and to remain. Most agree on the meaning of "gharam" as a constant, relentless suffering that does not leave the sinner; al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi cite verses by al-A'sha and Bishr ibn Abi Khazim. Ibn 'Abbas and others understand it as ruin or harm, and Abu 'Ubayda as destruction. Al-Hasan reports that every creditor parts from his debtor except the creditor of Hell, and Muhammad ibn Ka'b sees in it proof that God demanded from the unbelievers the price of His blessings, which they did not pay, so He made them enter the Fire. Al-Zajjaj holds it to be the severest punishment, while Ibn 'Atiyya and others read the word as a heavy and crushing burden. On the distinction between "mustaqarr" and "muqam", al-Razi explains that the first refers to sinful believers who settle there without dwelling permanently, and the second to the disbelievers. Others consider the two words synonymous, joined for emphasis or stylistic variety. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi see in this supplication a humble plea that reveals the servants' urgent need for divine mercy. Some attach the phrase to the words of the believers themselves, others to God's speech, and most judge both readings possible without preferring one.

This verse describes the servants of the Most Merciful who, when they spend, neither exceed the limit nor are stingy, but keep a just balance between the two. The commentators agree on this general idea of moderation, but differ on how to define extravagance and miserliness. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada, Ibn Juraij and Ibn Zayd, as reported by al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi, hold that extravagance is spending in disobedience to God, however small, and stinginess is withholding God's right; spending in obedience is not extravagance however large, and al-Tabari reports Mujahid saying that spending gold equal to Mount Abu Qubays in obedience would not be wasteful. Others, such as Ibrahim al-Nakha'i, whom al-Tabari adopts, understand extravagance as exceeding what is permitted and stinginess as falling short of what is necessary, so that one neither starves nor leaves one's family unclothed, nor spends so lavishly that people call it waste. Awn ibn 'Abd Allah defines extravagance as spending another's wealth. Al-Razi, al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi stress the balance between excess and meanness. Ibn 'Atiyya insists that the measure varies with each person's household and means. Most read qawaman with a fatha, meaning justice; Hassan ibn 'Abd al-Rahman read it with a kasra, meaning what suffices for the need.

This verse describes one of the qualities of the servants of the Most Merciful: they avoid the gravest sins, namely associating a other deity with God, killing a soul that God has forbidden to kill except by right, and fornication. It warns that whoever commits these acts will meet the requital of his sin. The commentators explain that athām means punishment; some take it as a valley in Hell, others as a well in Hell, others as the requital itself. The readings of the verbs yulqa and yudā'af vary, some in the jussive and some in the indicative, and each has a grammatical justification.

Most exegetes agree that these three sins are among the greatest transgressions, that their punishment will be doubled on the Day of Resurrection, and that their perpetrator will remain in torment, humiliated. Ibn Kathir and the majority hold that this eternal abiding applies to one who does not repent, and that the murderer's repentance is accepted. Ibn Kathir reads the verse of the Women on deliberately killing a believer as referring to one who does not repent. Ibn 'Abbas, in some reports, holds that the murderer who knew Islam has no repentance and that the verse is abrogated by the verse of the Women; others say it is decisive.

All agree that repentance, faith and righteous deeds are required. On the transformation of evil deeds into good, Ibn 'Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Hasan, Mujahid and Qatada take it to occur in this world, with polytheism becoming faith and fornication becoming chastity, while Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab and 'Ali ibn al-Husayn place it in the hereafter. Al-Zajjaj says the bad deed does not itself become good but is erased by repentance, and the good deed is recorded with it. Ibn al-Qayyim discusses the matter at length and concludes that repentance itself becomes a good deed that takes the place of the sin.

According to al-Tabari, the verse was revealed about polytheists who wished to embrace Islam, and according to others, about Wahshi, the slayer of Hamza. In sum, the verse affirms the gravity of these sins and opens the way back to God for anyone who sincerely repents.

This verse states that whoever sets up a partner with God, kills a soul that God has forbidden except by right, or commits fornication will have his punishment doubled on the Day of Resurrection and will remain in it humiliated. Commentators explain the word athām in different ways: al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and others take it to mean the penalty, while several report that it is a valley in Hell, and al-Suddi understands it as recompense. They agree that the verse names the three gravest sins and that the doubling reflects the addition of sins to shirk. On the meaning of remaining forever, some limit it to the one who associates others with God or combines these sins, while others take it as a very long duration. The exception that follows concerns the one who repents, believes and does righteous deeds, for whom God replaces his evil deeds with good ones. Ibn Abbas, Said ibn Jubayr, al-Hasan, Mujahid and Qatada link this replacement to this world, while Said ibn al-Musayyab and Makhul place it on the Day of Judgment. Al-Zajjaj holds that the evil deed itself does not become good but is erased by repentance. Readers differ on whether the verbs are read in the jussive or indicative. Ibn Kathir reports that some companions, including Ibn Abbas, held the verse about murder in Surat al-Nisa to abrogate this one, while others considered it unabrogated.

This verse makes an exception: those who repent, believe and do righteous deeds will have their evil deeds changed into good ones, for God is forgiving and merciful. The commentators agree that the exception covers those who repent of polytheism and of fornication. On the killing of a believer, most scholars, such as Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi, link the matter to the verse in al-Nisa' and say that it concerns the one who does not repent. Ibn 'Abbas, in a report cited by al-Tabari and others, held that a deliberate killer has no repentance, and some transmit that this verse was abrogated by the one in al-Nisa'. Al-Tabari, citing Ibn Zayd, notes that the doubled punishment and eternal abiding concern those who associate partners with God. As for the change of evil deeds into good, al-Hasan, Mujahid, Qatada and Ibn 'Abbas place it in this world: polytheism becomes faith, killing becomes restraint and fornication becomes chastity. Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab and Makhul place it on the Day of Resurrection, relying on the hadith of Abu Dhar. Al-Tabari prefers the first reading, while Ibn Kathir explains that repentance erases the sin and puts a good deed in its place. Al-Zajjaj holds that the evil deed itself does not become good, but is erased by repentance, which is accompanied by good.

This part of the verse says that whoever repents and does righteous deeds returns to Allah in a way that is accepted and pleasing to Him, erasing sins and earning reward. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir read it as a general promise of acceptance and mercy, and Ibn Kathir links it to other verses of forgiveness. Al-Razi argues that the repetition is not redundant: the first repentance is a turning away from disobedience, while the second is a return to Allah's judgment and reward. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi, al-Nasafi, Abu al-Su'ud and Ibn Juzayy stress that the return is accepted and that it wipes out sins. Al-Qurtubi notes that true repentance is shown through good deeds, not words alone. Al-Samani and al-Baghawi offer two readings: that the verse concerns repentance from sins other than those named earlier, or that it urges sincere repentance made for Allah's sake. Al-Tabari also reports that the wider passage was revealed in Mecca about pagans who doubted that Islam would benefit them after their crimes, and that some scholars regard the verse as abrogated by the verse on killing in al-Nisa, while others hold it to be firm. Several commentators, including Ibn Juzayy, present the phrasing as praise for the one who repents.

This passage of Surat al-Furqan describes another quality of the servants of the Most Merciful: they do not attend falsehood, and when they pass by idle talk they pass on with dignity, turning away from it. The commentators differ on the meaning of 'false speech' (zur). Al-Dahhak and Ibn Zayd, and Ibn 'Abbas in one report, take it to mean polytheism and the veneration of idols; Mujahid takes it to mean singing, and Muhammad Ibn al-Hanafiyya singing and amusement; Ibn Jurayj and Qatada take it to mean lying; Ibn Kathir also mentions the festivals of the polytheists and gatherings of vice, and Ali Ibn Abi Talha false testimony. Al-Tabari argues that zur is any falsehood made attractive and presented deceptively, so that all these meanings are included and none should be singled out. As for idle talk (laghw), al-Hasan understands it as all sins, Mujahid as the insults of the polytheists that one overlooks, and Ibn Zayd as the falsehood the pagans practised; Mujahid also reports that one avoided explicitly mentioning marriage. Al-Baghawi and al-Tabari report that Ibn Mas'ud passed by an entertainment, turned away from it, and the Prophet ﷺ said: 'Ibn Mas'ud has become noble.' Al-Razi and Ibn Kathir explain 'kiram' as nobility and dignity, like a generous she-camel that turns away during milking. Ibn Kathir, Ibn Juzayy and al-Nasafi hold that sitting in a gathering of sin amounts to sharing in it.

This verse describes the servants of the Merciful who, when they are reminded of their Lord's signs, do not turn away deaf or blind, but listen with attentive ears and look with seeing eyes. The commentators broadly agree on this meaning. Mujahid, Qatada, al-Hasan and Muqatil explain that they hear, see and understand the truth and what God reminds them of, while Ibn Qutayba speaks of people who do not feign ignorance of it, and Ibn 'Abbas sees them as fearful and humble believers. Al-Kalbi says they fall prostrate in listening and seeing. On the word 'yakhirru', al-Tabari holds that the negation falls on the deafness and blindness rather than on the falling itself, a view followed by al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan, who attach the negation to the condition rather than the act. Ibn 'Atiyya adds that falling here means collapsing without order, and al-Farra' explains that the sense is that they do not remain in their former state. Ibn Kathir contrasts these believers with disbelievers who, hearing the Quran, are not moved by it. Al-Qurtubi reports the view that whoever hears a reciter of a prostration verse should prostrate with him, but Ibn al-Arabi replies that this obligation generally binds only the reciter himself.

This passage describes the supplication of the servants of the Most Merciful, who ask God to grant them, from their spouses and offspring, that which delights their eyes: spouses and children who obey God and walk in His path, bringing joy to the heart. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, al-Hasan and Ibn Zayd explain that the believer sees his family obeying God; al-Hasan says nothing gladdens a Muslim's eye more than seeing a child, a grandchild or a close relative obey God. Ibn Juraij adds that they worship God and perfect their worship. Al-Tabari reports that some included in the prayer a wish to be reunited with them in Paradise, and al-Razi gives this as one of two interpretations. Ibn 'Abbas gives the example of a father seeing his son study jurisprudence. Al-Miqdad ibn al-Aswad recalls that in early Islam a son or wife could accept faith while a father or husband remained a disbeliever, so this prayer for their righteousness was a hope that comforted the heart.

As for the words "and make us an example for the God-fearing", most commentators understand them as asking to be leaders whom the pious follow in goodness, as Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada and al-Hasan say. Mujahid offers another reading: that believers follow the righteous who came before them and become guides for those who come after. Al-Tabari considers this a reversed construction. Grammarians differ on the singular word "imam": al-Farra' takes it as a singular used collectively, al-Akhfash as a plural of "amm", and others as a verbal noun. Al-Razi, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Qayyim take it to mean religious leadership, the pursuit of which is recommended, while Ibn al-Qayyim warns against seeking mere worldly authority.

This verse describes the reward of the servants of the Merciful mentioned before: they will be given the ghurfa, a high chamber in Paradise, because of their patience, and there they will be greeted with tahiyya and salam, abide forever and find it a good place to dwell and stay. The commentators broadly agree that the patience meant is general, covering obedience, restraint from forbidden desires and endurance of afflictions. Al-Dahhak restricts it to restraint from desires, Muhammad ibn Ali ibn al-Husayn to patience in poverty, while al-Razi extends it to the effort of reflection, the duties of worship, struggle and tolerance toward the polytheists. On the ghurfa, Ibn Abbas describes chambers of emerald, pearl and ruby, others take it as the highest levels of Paradise, and al-Dahhak as Paradise itself. The readings of yulaqqawna differ: al-Farra and al-Tabari prefer the form with a open yaa and light qaf for its common Arabic usage, whereas Abu Ubayd and Abu Hatim favour the doubled form, citing the verse 'wa laqqahum nadratan wa surura'; all agree the meaning is the same. Tahiyya is explained as a prayer for long life or lasting sovereignty, and salam as a prayer for safety from all harm, with the angels, God, or believers greeting one another cited as the source of the greeting.

The commentators explain that this verse closes the description of the reward of the servants of the Merciful, whose qualities have just been listed. They will be granted the ghurfa, understood by some as the highest chambers of Paradise and by others as Paradise itself, for their patience in obedience, in resisting desires and in enduring the harm of the disbelievers. They will be greeted with tahiyya and salam, which al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain as a wish for lasting life and freedom from every affliction, with the angels greeting them or the believers greeting one another. They will abide there forever, neither dying nor leaving, and this dwelling is a fine place of rest and residence, set against the Fire described as an evil place of rest and residence. Readers differ over yulaqqawna: al-Tabari and al-Farra' favour the form with a vowel and no doubling, while Abu 'Ubayd prefers the doubled form, though al-Tabari judges both as having the same meaning. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir report that the ghurfa is named for its height.

The next verse commands the Prophet to say to the disbelievers that his Lord would not care for them were it not for their invocation. Mujahid and Ibn Zayd read ya'bA' as "would act" or "would heed", Abu 'Ubayda as "would count you for nothing". Some understand the invocation as worship or faith, others as calling upon God in hardship. As for lizaman, most commentators, including Ibn Mas'ud, Ubayy ibn Ka'b and Mujahid, identify it with the day of Badr; Ibn 'Abbas takes it as death, Ibn Zayd as fighting, and others as the punishment of the Hereafter. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi note that these views can be reconciled. The commentators report these opinions without choosing between them.

The commentators explain that after describing the servants of the Most Merciful and their reward, this verse tells the Prophet ﷺ to say to people that God has no concern for them and gives them no weight, were it not for their worship and their calling upon Him. Scholars differ on the meaning of «ya'ba'»: Mujahid and Ibn Zayd take it as 'to do', Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' as 'to care', and al-Zajjaj as 'to have no weight'. On «du'a'ukum», Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Jurayj understand faith or worship, Mujahid understands God's call to His law, and others understand the supplication made in times of hardship. Ibn Kathir and most scholars favour the view that God created mankind to worship Him. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Alusi hold that the address is general, then narrowed to the disbelievers. On «faqad kadhdhabtum», most take it as denying the Messenger or the truth he brought, while others read it as falling short in worship. On «lizaman», Ibn Mas'ud, Ubayy ibn Ka'b, Mujahid and Ibn Kathir say it refers to the killing at Badr, Ibn 'Abbas says death, Ibn Zayd says fighting, and al-Hasan and Qatada say the punishment of the Hereafter. Ibn Kathir sees no contradiction, and Ibn 'Ashur holds that Badr is one instance of the promised, inescapable punishment, which also includes the Hereafter.
